description: I’m forming a team for a NASA space challenge: health monitoring software for astronauts. We’ll explore how easy-to-use software can track health data, reveal changes over time, and support informed follow-up during missions. I’m looking for teammates skilled in coding, software, web development, data analysis, data visualization, or design. Writing, communication, storytelling, and education can help make insights clear. Let’s build a practical tool to support astronaut health.
summary: Crew Check-In is a fictional-data prototype for exploring how astronauts could record everyday wellness information during a space mission. The app brings daily entries—resting heart rate, sleep, optional blood pressure and temperature, mood, hydration, meals, exercise, and notes—together in one place. Users can review past check-ins and see simple trends over time, helping them notice changes in their own records and mark an entry for medical-officer review. A Sources section links to NASA health and research resources that explain the spaceflight context. These sources are provided for background, not as universal medical thresholds. The prototype stores entries only in the user’s browser, uses sample data, and does not diagnose, provide medical advice, or generate health alerts.
details:
Introduction

CrewPulse is a browser-based prototype for recording and reviewing fictional astronaut wellness check-ins. It explores how a simple daily log could help crew members keep health-related observations organized during a long-duration mission. The prototype is for demonstration and learning; it is not a medical device and does not provide medical advice, diagnosis, treatment, or emergency alerts.

What the prototype does

  • Records daily check-ins: Users can enter fictional readings and routine details, including resting heart rate, sleep, mood, notes, and other selected wellness fields.
  • Shows check-in history: Saved entries appear in a dated list, so users can review what they recorded over time.
  • Displays trends: A chart presents recorded heart-rate and sleep values across check-in dates. It visualizes the entries; it does not interpret them as healthy or unhealthy.
  • Supports follow-up: A user can mark an entry for review. This is a way to identify an item for attention in the demo, not an automatic medical referral.
  • Provides a Sources section: The app links to NASA materials about human-spaceflight hazards and risks, plus measurement guidance from other health sources. These references provide context and measurement instructions; they are not used to claim NASA has set universal health thresholds for this prototype.
  • Includes measurement guidance: Short instructions explain how a user might take or record selected measurements. They are informational and do not replace professional guidance or mission procedures.

How it works

  • The user fills out the check-in form and saves the entry.
  • Entries are stored in the browser on the device being used. The prototype has no account system or central server, so data is not shared between devices.
  • The history and chart use the saved entries to make the user’s own records easier to review.
  • Sample entries are fictional and labeled as sample data.
  • No sensors, spacecraft systems, NASA databases, or external health services are connected to the app.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Makes routine wellness notes easier to record and revisit.
  • Presents information in a straightforward format that may help users notice what they have logged across multiple days.
  • Demonstrates how a small digital tool could organize self-reported information in a mission setting.
  • Encourages careful use of sources and clear communication about what a prototype can—and cannot—conclude.
  • Provides a starting point for discussion about usability, privacy, measurement consistency, and the needs of crews on long-duration missions.

Tools and development

  • Bolt.new was used to create and develop the web app.
  • The app was built with React and TypeScript, with styling and browser storage for the prototype’s interface and locally saved entries.
  • ChatGPT was used to help plan features, explain development steps, research and summarize source material, and draft project text.
  • The app contains fictional demonstration data. AI-assisted code and text are identified in the project’s Super Intelligence disclosure.

Design considerations

  • Clarity: Labels and short instructions aim to make the check-in understandable to a first-time user.
  • Privacy: Entries stay in the browser rather than being sent to an account or server.
  • Safety: The app avoids diagnosis, treatment recommendations, and unsupported claims about “normal” health values.
  • Source transparency: NASA resources are used for spaceflight-health context. Measurement instructions and any other external references are credited separately.
  • Prototype limits: The app has not been clinically validated and is not designed for real astronaut care or operational mission decisions.
